Eastern Cape Water Crisis

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With dams running dry and few alternative sources, cities and towns in the Eastern might reach "Day Zero" sooner than Cape Town.

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa's cyclical and perennial droughts, along with ageing and inadequate infrastructure, poor maintenance, planning and capacity constraints at local and government level, are being blamed for 'Day Zero" when taps run dry.

Summary:
In the Eastern Cape the Amatole district has been declared a disaster area with taps having run dry already. The Nelson Mandela municipality's combined dam capacity stands at 25.17%. It is possible that the Kouga dam will run dry in March leaving the metro dependent on the Nooitgedacht scheme which supplies only half the cities water. The scheme sources water from the Gariep dam through the Sundays River valley.the Nelson Mandela Bay municipality said nothing has been confirmed yet around "day zero.
Local and national governments lack of coherent water supply policy has contributed to the current crisis. Failing and inadequate infrastructure and poor maintenance has largely contributed to the water crisis. The towns of Patensie and Hankey have used all of their water quota and taps will dry run soon. The Department of Water and Sanitation had in 2017 slashed the authorized maximum withdrawal for use by Hankey and Patensie by 25%


Further information:
One of the Eastern Cape towns severely affected by a total infrastucture collapse is Grahamstown. It is the largest town in the ANC led Makana Local Municipality.
It hosts Rhodes university and the Eastern Cape Division of the High Court. It is the only town in SA whose primary commerce sector is that of education. Crumbling infrastructure, lack of municipal services and an alleged indifferent attitude by municipal officials have left residence with occurring water and electricity outages.Before Christmas there was no water supply for two days and no reply from the municipal office. Business and local investment confidence was virtually non-existent.
Grahamstown east (township) has their water cut between 17:00 and 07:00 in the morning. Taps have already run dry in Salem and residents only have access to water when delivered by truck. They often don't have water for up to three weeks at a time.

Press Release:


Eastern Cape Water Shortage
Ageing and inadequate water infrastructure, poor maintenance and planning, and capacity constraints at local and provincial government level could see Eastern Cape taps run dry very soon. In fact, it’s predicted that Day Zero may hit several parts of the Eastern Cape even before Cape Town. But why is nobody paying attention? Carte Blanche investigates the total infrastructure collapse in Grahamstown, systemic failures in Nelson Mandela Bay and elsewhere across the province.


Script:


MacFarlane Link




The Eastern Cape is in the grip of a serious water crisis. Dams like Kouga are running alarmingly low and with half of water lost due to infrastructure failure taps will be running dry soon.

V/O In the historic city of Grahamstown, residents have lived with water outages for many years. Nowhere is inadequate infrastructure, poor maintenance and planning more evident than here.
V/O On an ironically rainy day, Makana Municipality’s, Acting Manager, Ted Pillay, paints a grim picture
Ted Pillay interview



Title: Day Zero Based on the current calculations, we have one hundred and thirty two days in terms of our predictions to Ground Zero.









At the moment we are having tremendous challenges. The supply to the western side is highly constrained by the drought conditions that persist in the area, on the eastern side we do not have adequate supply to service the areas. That is due to the capacity of the water treatment works.

Would you say that bad governance especially from Provincial government has led you to here?

I don’t want to say that is the case.

But they have allowed it to go on for past five years?

I do not want to comment as such on that. But one thing I do know that in the past three years the provincial government has intervened tremendously.

V/O




Grahamstown East resident and social activist Ayanda Kota believes that the Makana municipality has failed the people.

Ayanda Kota: Interview It has been going on for years , you want to prepare the kids to go to school and then there is no water.
There are complaints up to this days that the people experience stomach problems and because of the water crisis as a result a number of people do not use the water of the municipality because of the contamination.
It is important to locate the discussion of the crisis of water within the context of the corrupt municipality.
V/O


Residents Association Secretary , Tim Bull, says the problem is twofold.
Tim Bull: Interview
On the western side, on the whole is where there are outages, breaks in the pipe, once its restored often its just full of mud and it can take days to settle down. On the other side of town it’s a different supply coming from sort of Lesotho , Orange river and that bears a lot of sediment which they have to try and get rid of. But I have heard people talking about the water smelling funny and getting ill because of it.






MacFarlane Link



V/O












Anthony Turton: Much has been reported about Cape Town and Day Zero but the situation in the Eastern Cape is just as dire with Day Zero arriving at an alarming pace.
Dam levels in the Nelson Mandela Bay area are continuing to decline. Comprising of 5 dams, the Algoa Water System level, has dropped to 25,6 % in comparison to 50,2% this time last year.

South Africa’s leading authority in water resource management, Professor Anthony Turton , says Day Zero is a reality.
.
Day Zero was that moment when the Titanic struck the iceberg . And we are now in that Titanic and the iceberg has hit, and the hull has got a hole in it but the Titanic is still floating. We don’t have dead bodies yet , but they are coming.



V/O


The province has been declared a disaster area and is racing towards catastrophe but Nelson Mandela Bay Executive Mayor,
Athol Trollip seems to think that there is no cause for alarm.
Athol Trollip: Interview













Anthony Turton: Interview






Athol Trollip: Interview

It’s a very delicate situation one doesn’t want to say we’re not going to reach day zero or that we are going to reach day zero. We saw that it created great panic in the City of Cape Town.
We are probably less likely to reach day zero than Cape town because we have major augmentation from the Gariep dam with the Fish River scheme but also we have a lot of underground resources, that we have already drilled, we have got productive boreholes.

The water that has been diverted out of the Orange river is not an infinite volume, we are reaching the limits of that available volume.

We rely on natural rainfall to supply water to the city, so we are in a precarious position. So I want to appeal to the people of Nelson Mandela Bay that the good habits we learn during the drought we must keep into future generations and teach our kids that water doesn’t come out of a tap , water comes from the sky into our dams into our infrastructure , into our homes, it’s a scarce resource.


Anthony Turton: Interview The fundamental problem in South Africa from a water resource management perspective is our conversion of rainfall to run-off . Of a 100 units of rain falling out of the sky at continental 20 units end up in the river at national level in South Africa of rain falling out of the sky only 8,6 units ends up in the river. In the Orange River Basin, its 3. Something.
We can’t squeeze another drop of what we have. All of our cities, particularly the coastal cities are on the end of rivers that have to a large extent been sucked dry by upstream inland users .Cities or farmers or whatever. To the extend that in Kzn you don’t get rivers flowing into the ocean anymore.



V/O Is the water crisis then not perpetuated by lack of municipal services, crumbling infrastructure and forward planning?

Athol Trollip: Interview No doubt.

What are we going to do about it?

The problem with any archaic system, you can patch but anytime you patch it and you turn the water back on it bursts somewhere else.
So the only way to really address that is to put in new infrastructure.




V/O
Although 45% of water is lost in the Nelson Mandela bay area through systemic failure,. Merely fixing infrastructure is not going to solve the water crisis in the long term. . Alternative sources such as desalination and water from recycling are urgently needed.
Athol Trollip: Interview
Desalinated water, Are there any plans afoot , what are you planning to do with regards to this.

We’ve got an initiative looking at a private public partnership on a small scale. There are a number of salt producing companies here in Nelson Mandela by. We are looking at putting it into our water reticulation system. So its one way so that’s one of the options. And then there are some other big companies that produce drinks to go into partnership with them, to make sure that they don’t run out of potable water.
We are going to start on a small scales with those pilots to see if we can use the ocean water and see if we can put it into our reticulation system. And I think it can work.


Anthony Turton: Interview
The economics of desalination, are very simple. The longer your capital payback time, the lower your unit cost. The bigger the volume through put the lower your unit cost. Its simple economics 101. So if now say that we are going to have lots of small plants you can never reach that magic number that makes it economically viable. That’s why you have 40, 50 Rand a kilolitre. And that’s what kills the whole desalination conversation.

Macfarlane
A Lot of experts are saying this is possibly the only option that you have for areas like Port Elizabeth as well as East London?


I refute that because we have other options and we are using those options now. But we are a coastal city and that gives us an extra sting to our bow. If things really get critical.

If you had to desalinate now, how much would you be charging for the water?

I can’t tell you that, because it’s not an option yet, and we haven’t done the scientific figures. I have seen that the figures are high.




Athony Turton: Interview What ill informed politicians will tell you when you ask them about it, first thing they will tell you, its too expensive. Compared to what? So in Cape Town we have now not used the too expensive option and we have destroyed the economy so the cost of resuscitating a destroyed economy the cost of restoring investor confidence the cost of a decade of lost production what is the cost now? And we know from Carte Blanche that the Israelis can offer water at 12 rand a kilolitre. But it gets better than that. With South African technology by blending desalinated sea water with water that comes from sewage, it can go down to R8-00. Lets call it ten rand a cubic metre. Is ten rand too much?


V/O







With a lack of progressive thinking and coherent policies at National Government level, the water supply to municipalities has been severely compromised
Athol Trollip: Interview A lot of the blame is been put at national government but we do know at some point municipalities also have to take responsibility,
But what role do you think they have played in letting some of these municipalities down?

Athol Trollip: Interview I know that I have the responsibility to provide water to every single persons home, that is my responsibility at local level I know that the national government has a responsibility to provide bulk water to the municipalities. To me, it is essentially about inter- governmental relations and sometimes it doesn’t work really well so we have to find ways of making sure that it works.
V/O But, sadly at grassroots level , the people of Grahamstown feel that the system at local and national level, has let them down.
Ayanda Kota: Interview
















V/O We have got councillors and officials, that I mean look here, they don’t show any empathy. The minister of water was here at some point, Minister Nomvula Mokonyana, All that he came to do was to lecture us and leave us then after and walked away. Without engaging us , without coming to the township and engaging the residents as to see what is the real water.
So they are not listening to the demands and the aspirations to the grievances of our people.


In reponse, Minister Mokonyana’s office released the following statement:
At no point has the Minister refused or avoided to engage with Communities and does so on a regular basis throughout South Africa. If there are community structures within Makana that would wish to engage, she’d gladly do so.




Athol Trollip: Interview Why hasn’t there been co-operation, what would you say is the problem?.



Macfarlane , I think that this has been a sobering example for all of us. That people expect government to keep taps running and the lights on and if they can’t do that there will be a consequence at the polls.
Ayanda Kota: Interview It’s also because they are saying that on the other side, the elite side, they pay rates. On this other side we don’t pay rates, I don’t know. If you don’t pay rates, does that take away your humanity? that I’m a full human being. I think that the crisis of water , that really dehumanises, it takes away your humanity

Promo 2 Its aging infrastructure like at Settlers dam which is more that 50 years old where Things like pumps have to be replaced. This is what lies at the core of the water crisis. 10”

Promo 3

The People of Grahamstown have lived with water cuts and failing infrastructure for a long time.

Unique Selling Point: South Africa's cyclical and perennial droughts, along with ageing and inadequate infrastructure, poor maintenance, planning and capacity constraints at local and government level, are being blamed for 'Day Zero" when taps run dry. Summary: In the Eastern Cape the Amatole district has been declared a disaster area with taps having run dry already. The Nelson Mandela municipality's combined dam capacity stands at 25.17%. It is possible that the Kouga dam will run dry in March leaving the metro dependent on the Nooitgedacht scheme which supplies only half the cities water. The scheme sources water from the Gariep dam through the Sundays River valley.the Nelson Mandela Bay municipality said nothing has been confirmed yet around "day zero. Local and national governments lack of coherent water supply policy has contributed to the current crisis. Failing and inadequate infrastructure and poor maintenance has largely contributed to the water crisis. The towns of Patensie and Hankey have used all of their water quota and taps will dry run soon. The Department of Water and Sanitation had in 2017 slashed the authorized maximum withdrawal for use by Hankey and Patensie by 25% Further information: One of the Eastern Cape towns severely affected by a total infrastucture collapse is Grahamstown. It is the largest town in the ANC led Makana Local Municipality. It hosts Rhodes university and the Eastern Cape Division of the High Court. It is the only town in SA whose primary commerce sector is that of education. Crumbling infrastructure, lack of municipal services and an alleged indifferent attitude by municipal officials have left residence with occurring water and electricity outages.Before Christmas there was no water supply for two days and no reply from the municipal office. Business and local investment confidence was virtually non-existent. Grahamstown east (township) has their water cut between 17:00 and 07:00 in the morning. Taps have already run dry in Salem and residents only have access to water when delivered by truck. They often don't have water for up to three weeks at a time. Carte Blanche HD michael@carteblanche.co.za 27 February 2018 Press Release: Eastern Cape Water Shortage Ageing and inadequate water infrastructure, poor maintenance and planning, and capacity constraints at local and provincial government level could see Eastern Cape taps run dry very soon. In fact, it’s predicted that Day Zero may hit several parts of the Eastern Cape even before Cape Town. But why is nobody paying attention? Carte Blanche investigates the total infrastructure collapse in Grahamstown, systemic failures in Nelson Mandela Bay and elsewhere across the province. Dams like Kouga are running alarmingly low and with half of water lost due to infrastructure failure taps will be running dry soon. V/O On an ironically rainy day, Makana Municipality’s, Acting Manager, Ted Pillay, paints a grim picture Ted Pillay interview Title: Day Zero Based on the current calculations, we have one hundred and thirty two days in terms of our predictions to Ground Zero. At the moment we are having tremendous challenges. The supply to the western side is highly constrained by the drought conditions that persist in the area, on the eastern side we do not have adequate supply to service the areas. That is due to the capacity of the water treatment works. Would you say that bad governance especially from Provincial government has led you to here? I don’t want to say that is the case. But they have allowed it to go on for past five years? I do not want to comment as such on that. But one thing I do know that in the past three years the provincial government has intervened tremendously. V/O Grahamstown East resident and social activist Ayanda Kota believes that the Makana municipality has failed the people. Ayanda Kota: Interview It has been going on for years , you want to prepare the kids to go to school and then there is no water. There are complaints up to this days that the people experience stomach problems and because of the water crisis as a result a number of people do not use the water of the municipality because of the contamination. It is important to locate the discussion of the crisis of water within the context of the corrupt municipality. V/O Residents Association Secretary , Tim Bull, says the problem is twofold. Tim Bull: Interview On the western side, on the whole is where there are outages, breaks in the pipe, once its restored often its just full of mud and it can take days to settle down. But I have heard people talking about the water smelling funny and getting ill because of it. Dam levels in the Nelson Mandela Bay area are continuing to decline. Comprising of 5 dams, the Algoa Water System level, has dropped to 25,6 % in comparison to 50,2% this time last year. And we are now in that Titanic and the iceberg has hit, and the hull has got a hole in it but the Titanic is still floating. We don’t have dead bodies yet , but they are coming. To the extend that in Kzn you don’t get rivers flowing into the ocean anymore. Athol Trollip: Interview Anthony Turton: Interview Athol Trollip: Interview It’s a very delicate situation one doesn’t want to say we’re not going to reach day zero or that we are going to reach day zero. We saw that it created great panic in the City of Cape Town. We are probably less likely to reach day zero than Cape town because we have major augmentation from the Gariep dam with the Fish River scheme but also we have a lot of underground resources, that we have already drilled, we have got productive boreholes. The water that has been diverted out of the Orange river is not an infinite volume, we are reaching the limits of that available volume. We rely on natural rainfall to supply water to the city, so we are in a precarious position. So I want to appeal to the people of Nelson Mandela Bay that the good habits we learn during the drought we must keep into future generations and teach our kids that water doesn’t come out of a tap , water comes from the sky into our dams into our infrastructure , into our homes, it’s a scarce resource. Anthony Turton: Interview The fundamental problem in South Africa from a water resource management perspective is our conversion of rainfall to run-off . Of a 100 units of rain falling out of the sky at continental 20 units end up in the river at national level in South Africa of rain falling out of the sky only 8,6 units ends up in the river. In the Orange River Basin, its 3. Something. We can’t squeeze another drop of what we have. All of our cities, particularly the coastal cities are on the end of rivers that have to a large extent been sucked dry by upstream inland users .Cities or farmers or whatever. To the extend that in Kzn you don’t get rivers flowing into the ocean anymore. V/O Is the water crisis then not perpetuated by lack of municipal services, crumbling infrastructure and forward planning? Athol Trollip: Interview No doubt. What are we going to do about it? The problem with any archaic system, you can patch but anytime you patch it and you turn the water back on it bursts somewhere else. So the only way to really address that is to put in new infrastructure. V/O Although 45% of water is lost in the Nelson Mandela bay area through systemic failure,. Merely fixing infrastructure is not going to solve the water crisis in the long term. . Alternative sources such as desalination and water from recycling are urgently needed. Athol Trollip: Interview Desalinated water, Are there any plans afoot , what are you planning to do with regards to this. We’ve got an initiative looking at a private public partnership on a small scale. There are a number of salt producing companies here in Nelson Mandela by. We are looking at putting it into our water reticulation system. So its one way so that’s one of the options. And then there are some other big companies that produce drinks to go into partnership with them, to make sure that they don’t run out of potable water. We are going to start on a small scales with those pilots to see if we can use the ocean water and see if we can put it into our reticulation system. And I think it can work. Anthony Turton: Interview The economics of desalination, are very simple. The longer your capital payback time, the lower your unit cost. The bigger the volume through put the lower your unit cost. Its simple economics 101. So if now say that we are going to have lots of small plants you can never reach that magic number that makes it economically viable. That’s why you have 40, 50 Rand a kilolitre. And that’s what kills the whole desalination conversation. Macfarlane A Lot of experts are saying this is possibly the only option that you have for areas like Port Elizabeth as well as East London? I refute that because we have other options and we are using those options now. But we are a coastal city and that gives us an extra sting to our bow. If things really get critical. If you had to desalinate now, how much would you be charging for the water? I can’t tell you that, because it’s not an option yet, and we haven’t done the scientific figures. I have seen that the figures are high. Athony Turton: Interview What ill informed politicians will tell you when you ask them about it, first thing they will tell you, its too expensive. Compared to what? So in Cape Town we have now not used the too expensive option and we have destroyed the economy so the cost of resuscitating a destroyed economy the cost of restoring investor confidence the cost of a decade of lost production what is the cost now? And we know from Carte Blanche that the Israelis can offer water at 12 rand a kilolitre. But it gets better than that. With South African technology by blending desalinated sea water with water that comes from sewage, it can go down to R8-00. Lets call it ten rand a cubic metre. Is ten rand too much? V/O With a lack of progressive thinking and coherent policies at National Government level, the water supply to municipalities has been severely compromised Athol Trollip: Interview A lot of the blame is been put at national government but we do know at some point municipalities also have to take responsibility, But what role do you think they have played in letting some of these municipalities down? Athol Trollip: Interview I know that I have the responsibility to provide water to every single persons home, that is my responsibility at local level I know that the national government has a responsibility to provide bulk water to the municipalities. To me, it is essentially about inter- governmental relations and sometimes it doesn’t work really well so we have to find ways of making sure that it works. V/O But, sadly at grassroots level , the people of Grahamstown feel that the system at local and national level, has let them down. Ayanda Kota: Interview We have got councillors and officials, that I mean look here, they don’t show any empathy. The minister of water was here at some point, Minister Nomvula Mokonyana, All that he came to do was to lecture us and leave us then after and walked away. Without engaging us , without coming to the township and engaging the residents as to see what is the real water. V/O So they are not listening to the demands and the aspirations to the grievances of our people. In reponse, Minister Mokonyana’s office released the following statement: At no point has the Minister refused or avoided to engage with Communities and does so on a regular basis throughout South Africa. If there are community structures within Makana that would wish to engage, she’d gladly do so. Athol Trollip: Interview Why hasn’t there been co-operation, what would you say is the problem?. Macfarlane , I think that this has been a sobering example for all of us. That people expect government to keep taps running and the lights on and if they can’t do that there will be a consequence at the polls. Ayanda Kota: Interview It’s also because they are saying that on the other side, the elite side, they pay rates. On this other side we don’t pay rates, I don’t know. If you don’t pay rates, does that take away your humanity? that I’m a full human being. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With dams running dry and few alternative sources, cities and towns in the Eastern might reach "Day Zero" sooner than Cape Town.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa's cyclical and perennial droughts, along with ageing and inadequate infrastructure, poor maintenance, planning and capacity constraints at local and government level, are being blamed for 'Day Zero" when taps run dry.
metadata.Summary: In the Eastern Cape the Amatole district has been declared a disaster area with taps having run dry already. The Nelson Mandela municipality's combined dam capacity stands at 25.17%. It is possible that the Kouga dam will run dry in March leaving the metro dependent on the Nooitgedacht scheme which supplies only half the cities water. The scheme sources water from the Gariep dam through the Sundays River valley.the Nelson Mandela Bay municipality said nothing has been confirmed yet around "day zero. Local and national governments lack of coherent water supply policy has contributed to the current crisis. Failing and inadequate infrastructure and poor maintenance has largely contributed to the water crisis. The towns of Patensie and Hankey have used all of their water quota and taps will dry run soon. The Department of Water and Sanitation had in 2017 slashed the authorized maximum withdrawal for use by Hankey and Patensie by 25%
metadata.Further information: One of the Eastern Cape towns severely affected by a total infrastucture collapse is Grahamstown. It is the largest town in the ANC led Makana Local Municipality. It hosts Rhodes university and the Eastern Cape Division of the High Court. It is the only town in SA whose primary commerce sector is that of education. Crumbling infrastructure, lack of municipal services and an alleged indifferent attitude by municipal officials have left residence with occurring water and electricity outages.Before Christmas there was no water supply for two days and no reply from the municipal office. Business and local investment confidence was virtually non-existent. Grahamstown east (township) has their water cut between 17:00 and 07:00 in the morning. Taps have already run dry in Salem and residents only have access to water when delivered by truck. They often don't have water for up to three weeks at a time.
